name: Salvadoran Spanish
notes: STRUCTURAL STUB. Salvadoran Spanish — Lipski's (1994) 'El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua' Central American zone; voseo, with a Nawat/Pipil (Nahuan) adstrate. Only the pan-Latin-American baseline (seseo, yeismo; Lipski 1994) is modelled; national-specific phonology not yet described (stub tier). WORD-FINAL /n/ IS VELAR [ŋ]: pan [ˈpaŋ], un otro [uŋ ˈotɾo]. Lipski (2011, p. 7): «Velarization of phrase-final /n/ is the rule in Galicia and parts of Asturias, Extremadura, Andalusia, the Canary Islands, all Caribbean and Central American dialects, along the Pacific coast of Colombia, Peru, and Ecuador, and sporadically in the Andean highlands. Word-final prevocalic nasals are typically also velarized in these dialects, although with generally lower rates than for phrase-final /n/ (Lipski 1986): un otro [uŋ.ˈo.tɾo]».

sources.notes: READ (geo.pdf). Reproduces the Lipski (1994) geographical dialect-zone classification of Latin American Spanish (list (2)): Mexican/SW-US; Caribbean; Guatemala-Yucatan-Costa Rica; El Salvador-Honduras-Nicaragua; interior Colombia + highland Venezuela; Pacific coast Colombia/Ecuador/Peru; Andean (Ecuador/Peru/Bolivia/NW-Argentina/NE-Chile); Chile; Paraguay/NE-Argentina/E-Bolivia; Argentina/Uruguay. Used here to enumerate the regional zones, and p. 7 for the velar word-final /n/.

location.notes: San Salvador. A national variety: the capital stands in for the country. [Wikidata Q3110 P625]

allophone_rules.notes: Lowland glottalisation: /x/ (⟨j⟩, ⟨g⟩ before front vowel) is the glottal aspirate [h], not the Castilian velar [x] (Lipski 1994).
Lowland coda /s/ lenition (aspiration tier of Lipski's 1994 cline): syllable-final /s/ (from ⟨s⟩ and seseante ⟨z⟩) weakens to the glottal aspirate [h] (esta=[ˈehta], los=[loh], diez=[djeh]).

sandhi_rules.name: word-final velar n before a labial
sandhi_rules.notes: Word-final /n/ is velar only before a pause or a vowel. Before a consonant of the next word it takes the place of that consonant, as inside a word. Lipski (1986, p. 140): «Velarization of /n/ normally occurs in word-final environments before pause (también [tambiéŋ] 'also') and usually before a following vowel (en agosto [eŋaɣósto] 'in August')», written as the rule n → ŋ / __ # [−cons]. Lipski (1986, pp. 146-147): «the velarization of word-final preconsonantal /n/ is relatively less common in most dialects (Zamora and Guitart 1982:116), and the velarization of word-internal preconsonantal /n/ is rarer still. This is due to the normal process of homorganic assimilation of nasal consonants to following obstruents», and «I know of no dialect nor even idiolect of Spanish in which the majority of instances of preconsonantal /n/ are velarized». Navarro Tomás (1918, § 87, p. 66) gives the labial case across words: «En contacto con estas mismas consonantes iniciales de palabra, la n final de una palabra anterior se pronuncia también m», un buen baile [um bwem baile], en pie [em pjé]. So the nasal is [m] before p b m (the set of the es-ES rule ES_NASAL_LABIAL inside a word), stays [ŋ] before a velar or a glide, and is [n] before any other consonant, the value es-ES gives a nasal before such a consonant inside a word (enfermo [enˈfeɾmo], ancho [ˈantʃo]).
